Series Doc Authoring Standard¶

This note records the standing style and quality bar for the handwritten Series API reference work in PlussQit/docs/sphinx/api/series.

Use this note as the working standard for every remaining Series page unless the user explicitly changes direction.

The repository-wide requirements in API_Doc_Authoring_Standard.md also apply. In particular, examples are a behavioral inventory: their count must expand to cover every overload and materially distinct branch rather than satisfying an arbitrary minimum.

Public Naming Rules¶

  • Public-facing names are Series, Note, and Timeline.

  • Do not surface internal coded names like coden, codem, or codeh in the prose unless a private/internal implementation note is absolutely unavoidable.

  • Do not teach through comparisons to other public libraries or APIs.

  • Do not mention names like torch, numpy, or similar external surfaces in these public docs.

  • Prefer public aliases over internal type spellings in signatures and parameter descriptions when the doc can do so cleanly.

  • Avoid exposing pluss::msharp in example code. If a public call site can be expressed without it, do that.

  • When printing a Series, prefer pluss::series::print(...) over the older flat helper spelling.

Prose Standard¶

  • Write with the goal of teaching the reader how to use Series in real projects, not just documenting that a method exists.

  • Explain each parameter, including every toggle and overload branch.

  • State what each toggle changes: shape, dtype, broadcasting behavior, axis semantics, mutation behavior, reduction behavior, gradient behavior, and failure behavior where relevant.

  • Distinguish clearly between: reduction vs transform, in-place vs out-of-place, comparison vs reduction, value-returning vs index-returning, global vs axis-wise behavior.

  • Prefer richer prose that teaches the mental model behind the method, not just a terse definition.

  • Add explicit “Gotchas And Failure Modes” sections where useful.

  • Add a short “Summary” section on load-bearing methods.

  • If a method has quirks, say so directly and concretely.

Example Standard¶

  • Every example must be verified against the real implementation.

  • The output goes directly under the example that produced it.

  • Use several examples in incremental fashion.

  • For larger surfaces with many overloads or richer behavior, use more examples. A sophisticated page may need 7-10 examples.

  • Escalate examples from simple to advanced: plain case, axis/toggle variation, broadcasting variation, negative dims, keepdim behavior, scalar vs Series behavior, in-place behavior, gradient behavior, tie behavior, error/failure behavior.

  • Do not include an example unless its output is known and verified.

Example Syntax Rules¶

  • Prefer brace-based make_series calls: pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}, {3}) not pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3}, {3}).

  • For 2D and nested examples, prefer plain brace lists when supported: pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}}).

  • If a parameter accepts range-like input, prefer ordinary brace usage or plain containers in the example instead of explicitly constructing internal RangeView/msharp wrappers.

  • Avoid teaching low-level internal construction patterns that would encourage users to program against internals.

Verification Discipline¶

  • Back every public example with a compiled-and-run demo when possible.

  • If a page is rewritten substantially, update or extend the backing demo first if the current coverage is too thin.

  • Use the real outputs from those demos in the page.

  • Re-run: docs/scripts/validate_doc_examples.py and the PlussQit Sphinx build after substantial page batches.

  • Keep previously known build warnings separate from any new regressions.

  • During long builds, do other productive local work instead of polling and repeating the same progress update. Only report when there is actual new information.

Page Structure Preference¶

For load-bearing Series methods, prefer this shape:

  1. Signature

  2. What It Does

  3. Overload Map, if needed

  4. Parameters

  5. Returns

  6. Gradient, if relevant

  7. Examples

  8. Gotchas And Failure Modes

  9. Summary

  10. See Also

Not every page needs every section, but this is the default standard.

Tone¶

  • Clear, direct, and teacherly.

  • Richer than terse reference prose, but still precise.

  • No fluff.

  • No internal-engineering leakage unless the behavior cannot be explained honestly without it.
